original_question: Prove that spike features arise in generic singular solutions of Einstein's equations and determine how those recurring spikes affect any eventual proof describing generic spacelike singularities.
target_in_paper: Problem P15 in §5.2 ("Cosmological singularities and spikes"): "Prove the existence of spikes and determine their effect on any eventual generic singularity proofs." This is the nearest official formulation matching the draft, rather than the neighboring Problem P14 on BKL locality or Problem P16 on structural stability for matter fields. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/710276968/Unsolved-problems-in-mathematical-physics))
correct_elements: Your draft gets the core target right: it asks for a proof of the existence of spike phenomena in singular Einstein dynamics and asks how those spikes affect any eventual proof of the generic spacelike-singularity picture. It also correctly places the issue in the setting of Einstein’s equations and generic singular behavior, not in a purely homogeneous or purely numerical subproblem. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/710276968/Unsolved-problems-in-mathematical-physics))
missing_details: The paper’s formal target is the open problem P15 in general relativity, stated in §5.2, not a broader claim that spikes arise in all generic singular solutions. The official wording is to prove the existence of spikes and determine their effect on eventual generic singularity proofs. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/710276968/Unsolved-problems-in-mathematical-physics))

The surrounding setting is generic inhomogeneous cosmology in GR near a past spacelike singularity, specifically in the BKL/mixmaster discussion of cosmological singularities. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/710276968/Unsolved-problems-in-mathematical-physics))

To make the question stand alone, the paper’s contextual definition of a spike should be supplied: a spatial point remains in an old Kasner epoch while neighboring points bounce to a new one, so spatial-derivative terms become significant there. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/710276968/Unsolved-problems-in-mathematical-physics))

The paper links spikes to a possible failure of asymptotic locality at isolated points or surfaces, so that contextual role should be made explicit if the question is to be fully paper-faithful. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/710276968/Unsolved-problems-in-mathematical-physics))

Your draft adds 'recurring' spikes, but recurring spike behavior appears in the paper only as a follow-up unresolved issue after P15, not in the formal statement of P15 itself. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/710276968/Unsolved-problems-in-mathematical-physics))

No ambient ring/field, polynomial degree, homogeneity, nilpotency condition, operator over a specified algebra, or phrases such as 'for all sufficiently large m' are relevant here; the missing precision is geometric and dynamical (spacetime class, singularity regime, and spike definition), not algebraic. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/710276968/Unsolved-problems-in-mathematical-physics))
refined_question: In general relativity, for generic inhomogeneous cosmological solutions of the Einstein field equations approaching a past spacelike singularity in the BKL/mixmaster regime, prove the existence of spike structures—namely spatial points that remain in an old Kasner epoch while neighboring points transition to a new one, so that spatial-derivative terms remain dynamically significant and asymptotic locality can fail there—and determine how the presence of such spikes must enter any eventual proof of the generic spacelike-singularity picture. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/710276968/Unsolved-problems-in-mathematical-physics))
justification: This draft clearly targets the spike problem in §5.2. The section first sets the BKL context for generic inhomogeneous cosmologies approaching a past spacelike singularity, then explains what spikes are, why they matter analytically, and how they may violate asymptotic locality at isolated points, and finally states Problem P15. Because 'recurring spikes' are mentioned only in the subsequent discussion of additional unresolved questions, the closest paper-faithful rewrite keeps the official task 'prove the existence of spikes' while importing only the contextual definitions needed to make the question self-contained. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/710276968/Unsolved-problems-in-mathematical-physics))
